# Diagnosing Intermittent Cranks in a 2008 Chevy Cobalt

A single click when turning the key, followed by silence, is the classic auditory signature of an electrical system that can't sustain the load required to fire the engine. In the case of your 2008 Chevy Cobalt, this symptom persisted for months before finally giving way to a total loss of power while driving. The sequence of eventsâlights fading, dashboard going dark, and the engine shuddering to a haltâsuggests a catastrophic failure in voltage delivery rather than a simple mechanical seizure.

You replaced both the battery and the alternator last week, which is the logical first step when facing these symptoms. However, the fact that the vehicle operated normally for only three days before returning to "click-no-start" behavior indicates that the root cause wasn't merely a lack of stored energy or a failing charge unit. The alternator's job is to keep the battery topped off while the engine runs; if it failed completely, the car would likely die immediately after turning off the ignition, not start up again after a few days. The rapid return to failure points toward either a parasitic drain that exhausted the new battery almost instantly or an underlying issue that prevents the starter from engaging reliably until specific conditions are met.

When you hear a single click but the engine doesn't turn over, the starter solenoid is engaging, but the motor isn't spinning fast enough to generate compression or fire the cylinders. This often happens when the voltage drop across the starter circuit exceeds a threshold where the internal brushes cannot maintain contact under load. In many GM vehicles of this era, corrosion on the battery terminals or a weak ground strap can create exactly this scenario. Even if you installed new components, if the connection points are dirty or loose, the high current draw of the starter will cause a voltage sag that mimics a dead battery.

The intermittent nature of the problemâwhere sometimes it starts right up and other times it takes 20 triesâis highly characteristic of a failing ignition switch or an issue with the crankshaft position sensor circuit. The ignition switch in older Cobalts is notorious for internal resistance buildup. As the contacts wear, they may provide enough voltage to spin the starter when the key is fresh out of the cylinder, but fail under load after repeated attempts. Similarly, if the Engine Control Module (ECM) isn't receiving a stable signal from the crankshaft position sensor, it will inhibit fuel injection and spark generation until the engine reaches a specific RPM threshold, causing that frustrating delay before the car catches.

To isolate the issue without immediately replacing expensive parts, start by verifying the battery health under load. A multimeter reading of 12.6V at rest is insufficient if the voltage drops below 10V during a starter test. If the alternator is functioning correctly (which it appears to be for a few days), check the ground straps connecting the engine block to the chassis. A corroded ground strap acts as a resistor, starving the starter motor of amperage when the engine is hot or under vibration.

If the connections are clean and tight, the ignition switch remains a prime suspect given the history of "clicks" and intermittent operation. The trade-off here is cost versus reliability: replacing the switch resolves the electrical resistance issue but requires disassembling the steering column, whereas replacing the starter motor might be cheaper if the solenoid is the only component failing. However, given the total loss of power while driving previously, ensure you haven't overlooked a blown fusible link or a loose main positive cable in the engine bay, which could explain why the dashboard lights died completely before the car stopped moving.
